Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of pressing and urgent necessity. All of Canada was shocked at the murder of yet another policeman in the city of Calgary. It was a further shock when the public was informed that the two main figures involved in this tragic weekend drama, William Nichols and John Gamble, were released on bail after having been charged with attempted murder and murder respectively. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. According to the research department of Amnesty International at least 6,000 persons in Uruguay, about one in every 450 of that country's 2.5 million people, is a political prisoner. During the last few years one in every 50 persons has been subjected to interrogation, arrest, imprisonment or torture. The rule of terror in Uruguay is brutal and as far reaching as
any in the world. I therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That our Department of State for External Affairs send a controlled and dignified appeal to President Bardaberry of Uruguay seeking an end to such monstrous crimes in his nation.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STUDY OF REFUSAL TO ACCEPT RESIGNATION OF MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion concerning a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Since, according to the basic rules of our judiciary system, a Canadian citizen cannot intervene in the affairs of a court concerning a case submitted to justice and acts illegally if he does, and since members of a government must not only abide by the same rules as every other citizen but should also make it a duty, as established authority, to set the example by taking on, as it were, the leadership of integrity, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the House discuss immediately the statement made Friday by the Prime Minister to explain his refusal to accept the resignation of the Minister of Public Works, with a view to finding out whether in fact the rule of law can guarantee that justice be done in a case in which politics are involved, such as "the judges' affair", which concerns the House, and also to discuss the need to set up strict rules of professional ethics for parliamentarians in this regard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The application of CNR to increase its passengers rates in Newfoundland is contrary to an announcement by the Minister of Transport on November 14, 1975 that all federal Crown corporations whose rates are subject to review or regulation by federal regulatory authorities will be subject to the government's anti-inflation guidelines. subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER CONSTITUTION PATRIATED BEFORE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the right hon. Prime Minister. We are lucky to live in a democracy, which enables us to have

March 15, 1976
Oral Questions
the parliamentary system we have here today, quite under the constitution.
Mr. Speaker, my question relates to the constitution. For the last three or four days, we have seen on television and heard over the radio the comments by provincial premiers who fear that the constitution which the Prime Minister is prepared to bring back to Canada will include amendments. I understand it is a matter of patriating the document to Canada and the Prime Minister as well as the Parliament of Canada, have no right to amend this constitution as long as both the provinces and the federal government will not agree. Therefore, to put it clear in the mind of Mr. Bourassa or Mr. Moores or anyone else in Canada, does the matter of bringing home the constitution include the matter of amendments or do we patriate the constitution with a view to amending it after discussions between the provinces and the federal government? I think that the Prime Minister owes it to the country and to himself to clarify the issue so that we stop fooling around with public opinion throughout Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER CONSTITUTION PATRIATED BEFORE AMENDMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the hon. member gives me the opportunity to shed light for the benefit of the public. I suspect he has a clear mind on this matter, but he is right to say that the declaration I made eight days ago was quite distorted. In answer to the hon. member and this can be checked by any member or reporter by refering to the text, I never said that I would act unilaterally. I said I would consult the provinces...

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER CONSTITUTION PATRIATED BEFORE AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER CONSTITUTION PATRIATED BEFORE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
So, hon. members are surprised. They just have to refer to the text rather than to newspapers. I very clearly indicated that I would continue to consult the provinces and that I hoped we would reach an agreement with all provinces and, if not, then the government should consider introducing a motion before both Houses so that Parliament could act without the provinces. It is important that this first point be understood.
As to the second point, once again, Mr. Speaker, I think someone is trying, for reasons I ignore, to distort my words. I never said that once the constitution is back home the federal government intended to act unilaterally to give itself more powers or take some away from the provinces. On the contrary, I said that we should first patriate the constitution and then, between Canadians, we should continue to discuss the issue of sharing powers rather than go on discussing like we have been doing for one hundred years, when we have not even have patriated the constitution. I hope my answer is clear. Perhaps the hon. member wishes to ask a supplementary question? I would be glad to answer.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER CONSTITUTION PATRIATED BEFORE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask a supplementary question.
As I understand, instead of speaking of the patriation of the constitution to Canada as such, the provincial authorities of Quebec and other provinces speak of the amendments which the federal government would like to bring to it unilaterally. Now, people are left to believe, and even

some newspapermen seem to be under that impression, that the right hon. Prime Minister wants to patriate the constitution and amend it unilaterally, while I understand that, first, if we patriate the constitution nothing will be changed and, second, if it is amended it will be amended once it has been brought back to Canada. So I would like to know if the Prime Minister fully agrees with this interpretation and if he can assure the House that there will be no constraint or abuse of power against any province once the constitution has been brought back to Canada.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER CONSTITUTION PATRIATED BEFORE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a position I explained very clearly to the premiers of all provinces, and which I also publicly stated. It is this: as the hon. member said, it is a question of bringing back the constitution without in any way giving more power to the federal government, nor less to the provinces.
The premiers know that because this was the subject of our meeting of last April. I will even go further, Mr. Speaker, if people wanted to understand, and say that in the present situation, legally-not on the basis of tradition, but legally-being the only one empowered to deal with Westminster, the federal government could change this separation of powers. It would not be wise nor politically profitable, it would not be in conformity with tradition, but it would be legally possible. If we do as I propose, this will no longer be legally possible.

The House resumed, from Monday, October 21, 1974, consideration of the motion of the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald):
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take the lead in establishing a world commission on food and resources, under the auspices of the United nations, to compile a comprehensive and regular inventory of the existing world foodstuffs and resources essential for sustenance; each nation shall be required to report annually (with quarterly amendments) on the state of its own self-sufficiency and on its ability to transfer key foodstuffs and resources to more needy nations; the commission shall have the authority to transfer designated food and resources from member nations equal in amount to their expenditures on defence.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF WORLD COMMISSION ON FOOD AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make on the motion. Most certainly it is a timely motion that the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) has put forward, but I think we must take a close look at it in order to ascertain exactly what is being asked, what is the cost of duplication of committees and services, and so on. The motion states that the government should take the lead in establishing a world commission on food and resources, under the auspices of the United Nations, to compile a comprehensive and regular inventory of the existing world foodstuffs and resources essential for sustenance.
What is being done in this regard at the present time? The world's shortage of food has attracted, over past months and years, the attention of many people. Many efforts have been made by other countries as well as Canada to try to solve the problem. In November, 1974, a world conference was held, with 1,000 representatives from 130 countries, determined at that time to find solutions to food shortages and the relatively slow pace of agricultural development to feed the four billion people who now exist in this world.
The courses of action proposed at that time to help increase food production include some of the following. First of all, it was proposed to make available large quanti-

March 15, 1976
Food and Resources
ties of agricultural inputs such as fertilizers, water resources, high-quality seeds and improved management, all of which are essential to upgrading food production not only in Canada but everywhere throughout the world, more specifically in the underdeveloped countries. Also put forward was the idea of an expansion of research resources so as to evolve an appropriate technology in given conditions.
We must realize that those conditions vary greatly throughout the world. In Canada food production is limited to a very narrow belt across the country owing to extreme weather conditions in the north. On the other hand, the United States is a large country, able to produce vast quantities of foodstuffs primarily because of the favourable climatic conditions which they experience. The same is true of many other countries throughout the world.
The Soviet Union is faced with much the same problem as we in Canada. Their climate restricts the production of food to a very narrow growing belt across that large country. Food production is also limited in the underdeveloped countries in Africa, Asia and South America. There are so many conditions that must be taken into consideration in putting forth a program that will allow peoples of the world down through the years properly to feed themselves. Suggested, also, was a comprehensive rural development program that involves the people, particularly the small farmer and landless worker, as well as a major increase in the small amount of funds available for investment in agricultural development. This was urged at the conference for all countries of the world, not just Canada and the United States.
It will be noted that all the proposals dealt with increasing food production in developing countries as a means of solving the world food shortage. This, of course, is one of the features I would be glad to see put into the motion. The underdeveloped countries must be encouraged and given practical assistance and every other kind of assistance that we and other developed nations can give them so as to increase the ability of the developing nations and the underdeveloped nations to produce food.
In his November 11 speech to the eighteenth session of the FAO conference in November, 1975, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) had this to say:
Over the next five years, the need for substantive increased food production in the developed countries will be of much greater importance for world food supplies than was thought at the beginning of the 1970s.
This was true then and it is true now. We refer these days to the oil powers of the world. In 1980 the power that will be of utmost importance to world development will not be oil power but agrapower. We have discussed in the House from time to time the importance of petropower and where petrodollars are spent, but we must also give clear and concise consideration to the agricultural producing nations of the world and the power they will have in their hands by 1980.
To solve the food problem, developing countries and the FAO must give high priority to agricultural and fisheries development and adopt policies which give adequate incentive to agricultural producers if real progress is to be made. We must also assure the agricultural producers not only of Canada but the United States, Russia and wherever

they may be, adequate returns for the work they do in producing the world's food that will be required and which indeed is required at the present time. Today there are admitted problems with the production of powdered milk, and in the matter of food storage of items like powdered milk, butter and agricultural and dairy products we must remember it is the farmer who pays the shot. The farmer has to pay for storage so that this food is available in times of crisis and need.
A top priority in the interests of all countries is to ensure the vigour of the world's economy. This requires from our standpoint an efficient agriculture which produces enough food for all. This cannot be done without providing a reasonable livelihood to the farmers of the world who over the next 15 to 20 years will be performing a task of the utmost importance to the whole world. We know that without farmers, without the tools of production and necessary incentives, food production will fall short of our growing needs.
Canada maintains that it is unwise to form another committee or commission on a worldwide basis-I think this is a correct decision-for the purpose of compiling more information on the inventory of world food stocks. A number of commissions are already in existence to do that. Their purpose was underscored by events at the World Food Conference.
First, experience has shown that some countries cannot, or perhaps will not, make reports about food stocks. While there is a reporting system, unless there is one which all countries follow and use, and unless there is a complete reporting on the food stocks, that reporting system will not function properly. I am glad to note that Canada has always co-operated in making known our position in respect of food stocks and our ability to meet food aid targets. However, this is not the case in respect of some other countries.
Second, the government opposes the creation of new institutions, especially when there are institutions already in existence that seem able to do the work requested. In this connection, I would point out that four new committees or councils have recently been established. They are designed to work on specific problem areas yet interact with one another toward a common objective.
One committee I might mention is the World Food Council which has governmental representation at the ministerial level. This council is designed to deal with the political aspects of the food problem. It will receive regular reports on the world trade situation and on progress of food exports to developing countries. Another new committee is one that will be reporting to the World Food Council. I refer to the Committee on World Food Security. This committee will submit periodic and special reports on such things as current and prospective supply and stock positions of basic foodstuffs, the adequacy of stock levels and the evaluation of governmental actions to implement proposals on world food stock security.
Another committee, restructured from the World Food Program Intergovernmental Committee, is the Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programs. In our view, this will serve as a forum to improve co-ordination between bilater-

al and multilateral food aid programs. It will periodically review general trends in food aid requirements and food aid availability and will make recommendations to the various governments on food aid policies and operations.
While this is a very worth-while motion, it is simply an attempt to set up another committee to be stacked on top of other already existing committees which can provide the information that is being requested by the hon: member for Egmont in his motion. Also established is the consultative group on food production and investment. This group reports on activities to increase, co-ordinate and improve efficiency of financial and technical assistance to agricultural production in developing countries. This is of great importance in respect of the stocks of food in the world and the stocks that will be in the world.
Information in respect of technological advances in the developing countries is important because it may well be we would say to the people in China, Asia or India that they should eat more wheat but they still must be able to grow this wheat. It would also mean a switch in their basic diet, which now is mainly rice. If we ask such a person to change his eating habits and consume larger quantities of wheat, whether in the form of flour or other finished products, I think we would be taking a lot for granted. We cannot expect this to be done overnight.
When one considers the work being carried out by the Food and Agricultural Organization, plus the work that these new groups will be engaging in, I am sure all hon. members of this House will readily see there is substantial activity already under way to cover the very areas mentioned in the motion. It would be a needless duplication of effort to formulate another worldwide commission to deal with the very aspects now under study by these capable commissions of FAO.
I would also like to point out that the FAO has an international undertaking on world food security that deals in large measure with the very points covered by this motion. I should like to review the common purposes and responsibilities of this undertaking. The undertaking states that to assure a minimum level of world food security, member governments of FAO must take measures to ensure an adequate level of cereal supplies in the world so as to avoid acute food shortages in the event of widespread crop failures or natural disasters. To meet this objective, the members pledge to follow stock policies which in total will maintain at least a minimum safe level of basic food stocks in the world.
Member governments will also review or establish national stock targets or objectives with the aim of keeping sufficient levels to cover domestic and export requirements, including a security margin in case of disaster in a given country such as Canada. I am sure many members will remember the dust-bowl days on the prairies with very few fond memories. That was agreed to by Canada. It has also been agreed that the stocks will be maintained at such a level as will provide for emergency situations in all parts of the world where people may be less fortunate in recovering from a disaster. The member governments have also pledged to take measures to make sure stocks are replenished whenever they have been drawn below minimum levels.
Food and Resources
It is of the utmost importance, if emergency assistance is to be provided with any hope of help, that we have information on stockpiling so that the supply will not go below a certain level. Member nations agree to furnish, on a regular basis, information on national stock levels, government stock holding programs and policies, current and prospective export availability and import requirements for cereals and relevant aspects of the supply and demand situation. Such a situation arose just last year in the Soviet Union. A much larger wheat crop had been expected, as well as an increase in livestock production. Now, however, that country has found itself in a position where it must bring in new orders of Canadian and American stocks in order to cover the inadequacy it experienced during the past year.
To meet these requirements for timely and adequate information, a global information and early warning system on food and agriculture has been established under FAO supervision and operation. The main aims of the system are, first, to monitor continuously the world food supply and demand conditions, including fertilizers and key inputs, so as to assist governments in taking timely and appropriate measures in the light of quickly changing conditions. It is interesting, when I look at our friends in the opposition, to see that almost none of our socialist friends in the NDP have considered the problem of world food stocks to be of sufficient importance to be here and take part in the debate.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF WORLD COMMISSION ON FOOD AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion put forward by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) is still of current interest, even though the World Food Conference which was held in November 1974 did provide a specific solution to that problem by laying the foundations for joint action in trying to solve the problem of world hunger. In addition, apart from that World Food Conference, the 7th special session of the United Nations General Assembly which met in New York last fall, reiterated its full endorsement of the resolutions adopted at the World Food Conference. The twofold objective of these resolutions was to cope adequately and immediately with the crises that regularly develop in the world and, in the long run, to increase the food production of the developing nations.
In order to achieve this twofold objective, the Conference has asked the developing countries to supply food assistance totalling 10 million tons of cereals each year for the next three years. In order to build up this world food bank, the Conference has recommended the setting up of a variety of agencies such as the World Food Council, the International Fund for Agricultural Development, the Advisory Group on Food Production and Financing and the addition of a Committee on Food Assistance Policies and Programs within the World Food Program. Under the same program, the Special Assembly of the United Nations also suggested setting up an assessment committee of world food resources which would see to the creation of world stocks of cereals and would compile statistics on both needs and food production to avert emergency situations like those we have witnessed in the last few years.
In addition, one should mention the international agricultural research advisory group which also studied very specifically the best means of avoiding recurrent crisis situations. The committees I have just mentioned generally come under the FAO and should all contribute toward increasing food production in developing countries.
I shall not insist further, Mr. Speaker, on the various mechanisms that exist throughout the world and which were set up as a result of the World Food Conference. I believe they will meet the aspirations of the hon. member for Egmont who advocated an international organization to meet the food needs of the world community.
I should like to elaborate on this and direct mainly my

remarks to the Canadian reactions to the various resolutions passed by the Rome Conference, and the conferences held in Rome and in New York last fall. First, allow me to mention that Canada played a prominent role at the food conference and that since then its representatives have been working closely at the establishment of authorities and various committees recommended by the conference and that Canadian government officials still take an active part in setting up all those committees. To illustrate this Canadian participation, I wish to point out that Canada is one of the founding members of the World Food Council.
Moreover, Canada, through the Canadian International Development Agency, has geared its aid program to meet the urgent or long term requests in the agricultural field. Then, Canada's short term action as regards world food problems is more or less as follows: At the conference itself, Canada pledged 1 million tons of grain per year for the years 1975. 1976, and 1977, out of the 10 million tons requested by the Conference yearly. It is fair to say that this commitment has been a decisive factor in urging other donors to make firm commitments.
Canada, which has already endorsed the concept of a world food reserve, is now working within various international organizations to define the modus operandi of this reserve. And later in my speech, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with the interesting suggestion we find in the motion introduced by the hon. member for Egmont, namely that food assistance could be in some way related to the budget of national defence of the donor countries,
Canada has also undertaken to provide food assistance this year for up to $45 million, excluding grains but including fertilizers. Our food assistance program is increasingly being implemented through multilateral organizations such as the World Food Program and UNICEF in an effort to reach the most needy people in the developing countries. These organizations have shown their ability in the past to stimulate the authorities of these countries into accelerating their own agricultural development. Even if we are increasingly relying on multilateral organizations to convey our food assistance, the greatest part of it, namely 60 percent in 1975-76, is still being provided under bilateral agreements. To stress the importance of food assistance in the Canadian Co-operation Assistance Program, I would say that 30 percent of the budget, namely $255 million in 1975-76, were allocated in that area.
In the long run, the Canadian government's action in terms of food assistance could be summed up as follows: food assistance is only a short-term paliative, and according to the Canadian government and to experts development of the Canadian agency, only increased agricultural production in developing countries could resolve in the long run the world food shortage.
So, the new Canadian "Strategy for International Development Cooperation", for the period 1975-80 will stress better living conditions for peasants by promoting the extension of rural development programs, especially in agriculture, forestry and fisheries.
This trend will encourage not only the programs of agricultural production and infrastructure, but also those in research. By agricultural infrastructure, we mean upgraded rural electrical power grids, for instance, access
March 15, 1976

roads, land irrigation projects, programs for setting-up agricultural credit, a forest inventory and retimbering programs.
Canada has always considered agricultural research as one of the principal means to deal on a long term basis with the chronic food shortages of the most deprived countries. This research represents for those populations the determining factor of improved living conditions because it makes it possible to find permanent solutions to their problems and is likely to yield such economic benefits that those countries may hope to become self-sufficient some day.
Canada continues to support the research bodies of the third world, of which I shall list a few: For example, Canada provides funds for the International Development Research Centre in Ottawa, as well as for the International Institute for Tropical Agriculture in Nigeria. There are also funds made available by the Canadian government to the International Research Institute on Agriculture in semi-arid tropical areas in India. And we are also involved in the International Centre for the study of the potato in Peru. Moreover, we have made a financial contribution to the International Research Laboratory on animal diseases, an international government agency in Kenya. In addition, we participate in the West Africa Association for the development of rice production. And I could also mention, Mr. Speaker, organizations like the International Centre for Tropical Agriculture in Colombia, the International Centre for the Improvement of Corn and Wheat in Mexico, and the International Research Institute on Rice in the Philippines.
I therefore believe, Mr. Speaker, that international authorities have created adequate structures to try and solve the problem of feeding the hungry, and that we should be proud of the leadership given by Canada under these circumstances.
Mr. Speaker, I now return more specifically to the motion of the member for Egmont who suggests in the latter part of his motion the establishment of a commission which shall have the authority to transfer designated food and resources from member nations equal in amount to their expenditures on defence. So, if I understand, this part of the motion of the member for Egmont means that the countries which would be on that international commission and could create a food bank would be urged to provide food assistance in a proportion equal to their expenses for defence. This idea seems very interesting to me even though it might be difficult to implement, because if we ponder for a moment over the amount of money spent for military hardware across the world, we find that unfortunately these expenses result in an enormous wasting.
In 1974, for instance, the trade of conventional weapons exceeded $20 billion across the world. The industrial nations have earmarked an average of 8 per cent of their national budget but the average is rather low in Canada, when it is noted that some industrialized countries have allotted 18 to 20 per cent of their budgets. Now an average of 8 per cent of the gross national product is set aside for armament, while not a single one of those industrialized countries or only a few seem to have set 1980 as the year to reach 0.7 per cent of assistance which is the objective of the United Nations.
Food and Resources
Total world expenditures for armament, Mr. Speaker, are 30 times higher than development aid. The armament budget represents a percentage so high in comparison with our limited resources that it prevents us from coping with urgent economic and social problems in our industrial communities as well as in underdeveloped countries.
I think, as the member for Egmont seems to suggest in his motion, that it is essential that we take efficient steps for disarmament. In my opinion, we must extend the motion of the hon. member for Egmont which deals more especially with food assistance and cover the entire issue of the arms race throughout the world and we, parliamentarians, must try to drum up support among our colleagues and our electors for the importance of disarmament throughout the world. Mr. Speaker, I believe that even if this might seem utopian, the emphasis should be shifted from weapon sales to development assistance and that this is an ideal that we should try to reach. This is why I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Egmont for having proposed this motion relating development assistance to the defence budget.
However, there are very serious obstacles to disarme-ment if we think of all our military agreements, that is NATO on the western side, and the Warsaw Pact on the eastern side. It is unthinkable that those two military pact will have disappeared in five or even ten years. However, especially now when we are discussing a new world economic order, I believe that we should all stop and think how we could best achieve a shift from our present armament efforts to development assistance. I am convinced that with the good will of all the affluent people, and I am talking especially about parliamentarians, of all the people who have any influence on the international scene, if all parliamentarians make an effort in this direction, we shall be able to find solutions to the difficulties that we will meet when we try to put a stop to the armament race.
I therefore believe that it is our duty to galvanize, and I quote, Mr. Speaker:
To galvanize the world community towards more direct and more efficient action to stop the armaments race and change its orientation.
Former United Nations Secretary General U Thant said these words in 1966,1 think.
Therefore, in my opinion, in view of the moral implications and the possibility that we could meet such an objective in the long term, we must start the fight for disarmament as soon as possible. We must also impress the importance of food assistance on industrialized countries, as well as developing countries, which very often, urged by industrialized countries, unfortunately enter the armament race with great enthusiasm.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Egmont succeeds one day in dividing or extending his motion so as to relate general assistance problems to world disarmament problems, I would be happy to support such a motion if he should propose it.

Mr. Speaker, ever since I have been a member of this House I was always surprised when we had to consider a motion similar to the one that is now before the House that there was not unanimity and

March 15, 1976
Food and Resources
the House did not simply adopt, it. That was always a surprise, as I say, since reading the motion is of course admitting it, just thinking about what it implies is admitting it even altogether.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take only a few minutes to submit brief arguments on the necessity of accepting such a thing. A list was just given of a whole series of things involving Canadian participation. In fact, it was nearly said that it is now being done, that there are world agreements sponsored by the United Nations or international organizations, so that what is called for in this motion is currently being done.
Mr. Speaker, one must be realistic and see things as they are. What do we see now when a country like ours is faced with a food surplus problem and cannot find any solution? That is the situation at present in the field of agriculture. While a general trend of the agricultural policy for industrial milk producers is being justified, a trend that goes against the interests of those Canadian producers is being justified by saying: Unfortunately, we cannot get rid of those products in Canada, and we cannot either get rid of them abroad. Mr. Speaker, I said on many occasions-and I take this opportunity to repeat it-it is a sacrilege, a scandal to talk about food surpluses when we know that one third of the world is literally starving to death.
The motion is presented at a time when we could help those who in the world are having difficulty living because they cannot find all the food they would need. There should be one organization in charge of this inventory, in order to record what we have and and what could be exchanged between countries, and of course this should not be only a simple wish but something which should have been already realized.
Mr. Speaker, it is rather odd to speak about world food needs while declaring that we cannot find an outlet for our surplus of food supplies. As recently as last week, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was saying in answer to a question that our producers were badly organized, produced too much and were too efficient.
Mr. Speaker, I read just recently that here in Canada the consumption of essential goods was insufficient to ensure a healthy balance. At the moment, in our country for example, the consumption of dairy products is not sufficient.
Consumption should be increased in that area. I do not say that only to solve the industrial milk producers' problem but also our underconsumption problems since here in Canada we are faced with poverty. Mr. Speaker, we must not make a secret of it, but face the situation.
We should proceed to a very concrete, very real inventory of our possibilities in order, first, to help Canada, then our own consumers and also all countries of the world which need it. It is not merely a wish, it should be all hon. members' avowed intention.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak on the motion before the House. It seems to me, on reading the motion proposed by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), that it closely resembles another motion the House debated on an allotted day. I think the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) raised the matter. Many of the

arguments advanced that day in support of that motion are relevant in the present debate. I appreciate this opportunity to raise a couple of matters.
The previous speaker mentioned several things which, in my view, illustrate difficulties we might encounter if we accept this motion. If time permits I shall return to that topic later. The difficulties we could encounter are serious. They merit long and careful consideration. We should not lightly adopt the motion proposed by the hon. member.
The historic conference in Rome on world food supplies was convened about one year ago. Fortunately in the past year there has been an improvement in world food stocks. Conditions are somewhat better in areas formerly stricken with famine. At the same time there is little over-all improvement in the world crop and there has been little opportunity for rebuilding the world's depleted food reserves. Food shortages were the gravest concern facing the world's developing countries last year. We were all worried about the small reserves of world food. There was only enough food to feed the world for a few days. If there had been any disaster, or more drought, the consequences would have been serious indeed. That is not to say that the world food shortage is not still critical and that we should not do everything possible to improve world food stocks.
Before disagreeing with the hon. member for Egmont may I congratulate him for putting forward this motion? He has moved similar motions in the House on a number of occasions. I know he speaks on the subject with conviction. I congratulate him on it. I take issue with some of the points he raised today. I took issue with similar points which were raised on an allotted day. In short, I take issue with the means by which he seeks to achieve his aims.
The hon. member proposes that this House should urge the government to press for the establishment of a world commission on food and resources under the auspices of the United Nations. He further proposes that this commission should undertake broad responsibility for maintaining an inventory of world food supplies, for maintaining a reporting system on world food needs and availabilities, and for arranging an annual transfer of food resources from have to have-not countries. The value of the food transfer, he suggests, should equal what the have nations spend annually on defence.
The implication of this proposal which I find hardest to accept is that it involves the establishment of a new, major international body which would be of large proportions and whose functions would duplicate those of other large bureaucracies. Its functions would duplicate activity already being undertaken by other institutions both within and outside the United Nations, as one hon. member said.
Before agreeing to adopt the motion we should reflect carefully on whether we need another large bureaucracy to do something already being done. Do we need another large, powerful organization like that? I say this, because the motion reads in part:
... the commission shall have the authority to transfer designated food and resources from member nations ...
What does that operation involve? It seems easy to do it, but is it that simple? Really, transferring food from one country to another is just about the most complicated thing you can do. Consider the past history of such opera

tions. They involve shipping, storage, and payment of storage costs. They involve the payment of compensation to producers. I am most concerned about compensation to producers. If you analyse the motion, it suggests that we should ask farmers to produce food and then donate it to the world's needy. I would not want to see the farm community shoulder this kind of responsibility on behalf of all Canadians.
Other problems I foresee involve policies and programs of national governments, and the overlapping jurisdictions of international bodies. In relation to the latter point, liaison between these bodies would require a larger establishment just to negotiate the politics that would be involved. If actual operations-procurement, transport, distribution-also fell under the commission's jurisdiction, the staff and facilities required would be enormous, and so would its budget. I have not even come to the question of compensation yet.
I know the forces that play on a situation like this. In my constituency, a year ago last crop year, we had an early frost. Thousands of acres of potatoes were slightly frozen. There was a good deal of urgency with respect to what could be done about the situation. The growers approached the government to see if there was some program under which they could qualify. They made the point that many countries around the world would have a need for powdered or flaked potatoes, or potatoes in some other form like that. They were amazed to find it would cost more to prepare the potatoes in that form to be used by people who have the need than what the potatoes were worth, or that they could procure that protein food value a good deal closer to where the need was at a considerable smaller cost.
The previous speaker mentioned the situation in the dairy industry today. Admittedly there is a very large surplus, not only in this country but in the United States and most of the European Economic Community countries. He stated we should have a very high social conscience and distribute dried milk powder in great quantity to many of these countries. That is an over-simplification of the argument. In many countries that have a need, this is not a type of food that they use. In fact it might do damage to the health standards of people there.
This was established in the Guatemala situation. Canada distinguished herself by the amount of aid that was sent there; some $3 million worth of material for the construction of temporary shelters for about 40,000 people, some 125 tons of food, and another three quarters of a million dollars for emergency aid. The point there was the kind of aid that could have been given by sending more dry skim milk powder. That would have been easy for us to do. It would have decreased inventories and assisted our dairy industry. However, it would have been counterproductive to the people there. They are not used to that form of food in their diet. If it were all of a sudden to become a part of their diet, many problems could arise. In fact we might even contribute to the problem rather than help it.
I just wanted to make that point because I think the previous speaker over-simplified how easy it is to take any surplus commodity in our agricultural community and give it to the world food aid program. I am sorry he is leaving
Food and Resources
the Chamber. I wanted to ask him who he intended would pay for that, and whether in fact he thought that was an assistance to the program rather than working to the detriment of the people.
Having some background in the agricultural industry I feel somewhat strongly about it. If you have a situation that we often argue in this country where we have a surplus of food, and the producers say to the government it should buy it and give it to countries which need it, while that may have some short-term benefit, in the long run it might well harm the basic agricultural industry in the country we are trying to assist.
I ask hon. members to contemplate the effect in this country if we were trying to establish an agricultural industry in a particular sector and if another country with a surplus moved a lot of its food into this country. It might be good in the short period for consumer prices and even the nutrition of people. However, it would set back our own industry to the point where it might not even develop and in fact might be destroyed. As a result we would be further away from being self-sufficient in food rather than being closer to it. This is particularly important in the developing nations.
I had the opportunity to discuss this point of view at some length with some of my classmates who, in the last few years since our graduation, have spent a good deal of time in the developing countries. They are supplying technical assistance and knowledge to the government of those countries to see if they can help them become more self sufficient. Most of them have come back from their tour of duty from the underdeveloped countries unanimous in their point of view that perhaps the worst thing we can do as a country in assisting others is to send in large amounts of food. That would work to the detriment of those countries developing their own agricultural industry and achieving their goal of becoming self-sufficient.
I realize that in the motion, if I read it correctly, the hon. member is not suggesting that we override the attempts of underdeveloped countries to establish their own agricultural industry. He is really making the point that we move in areas of real need. We all have a great deal of sympathy with that. Whenever a crisis or a real need arises, one of the biggest problems is the time lag between the need arising and the time people can respond.
The hon. member's point in terms of having some type of data bank to indicate where certain food is available in surplus situation and can be moved very quickly, is probably the strength of the motion. I always worry when there is a great need, even in the Guatemala situation, about the length of response time.
Experience shows that it takes a long time to research within a country as to what it can best do. I suggest the hon. member has a good point and that maybe the reverse side is just as important. It is just as important for countries that are not strong agriculturally to have an inventory of the types of food they can most readily use. I would argue that this might be even more important.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when my speech was interrupted at five o'clock by the private members' hour I was in the process of explaining to the House that Bill C-68 applies to expenditure capping by the federal government under the medical care program and that it had nothing to do with the hospital insurance program in which the federal government participates on a 50 per cent basis.
I indicated also that the 13 per cent capping did not apply to any particular province but that it applied to the federal share of the program. It could happen, therefore, that if some provinces controlled their costs effectively they would receive more than 13 per cent. Provinces with lesser revenues could receive a way more than 50 per cent, and they could receive more than 13 per cent if they are effective in controlling their costs.
I should like to deal briefly with the arguments put forward by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). I regret to say I see few members of his party in the House this evening. He made a plea that the government should increase its expenditures to cover alternatives which would be of long term benefit. In other words, they would constitute a social investment. Mr. Speaker, that is precisely what the government is attempting to do. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has made a commitment to the provinces, restated by the former minister of finance last year, that the federal government is prepared to extend cost-sharing in alternative areas provided the federal government can obtain a firm commitment from the provinces to restrain the rate of escalation of costs in the hospital-medical field.
Over the past year we have held discussions with the provinces on many of the lower cost options mentioned by

the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, for example, increased use of paramedical care and institutional care at lower cost. The hon. member made a great deal about the need for community clinics. I would mention to him, though he be in absentia, that nothing in the Medical Care Act prevents such a development. What we have to get at is the hospital insurance program and provide for those kinds of institutions toward whose cost the federal government can participate. It should follow that the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby supports the Minister of National Health and Welfare in giving formal notice to the provinces that five years from June 23 last we will review that particular program with the provinces so that we can do the sort of thing the hon. member has in mind.
In addition, the new amendments provide an exemption from the ceiling for the first three years of any new extension of benefits under the act. They provide further that any ceilings which may be imposed after the third year can be varied according to the nature of the service provided. Thus the federal contribution in respect of each class of new insured service will be appropriate to the cost of that program and not simply averaged in with all other services covered by the act.
In conclusion may I say that in my view the government is not one which wants to restrict social expenditures.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want the hon. member for Gloucester
March 15, 1976

(Mr. Breau) to go away from this debate believing that all the people on this side of the House are completely without intelligence. When he says this bill deals only with medicare and not with hospitalization I would point out that the biggest cost in medicare is, as he said, payments to medical doctors. But without these medical doctors filling up our hospitals with patients we would not be in the mess we are in presently. Therefore there is a very tight connection between medicare and hospitalization.
The main point I want to make is that here we are engaged in a debate under an allocation of time order and, whether we call it this, or that, or the other thing, it is still part of a closure operation. What the opposition has been doing is attempting to convince the government that we in opposition are trying to help it make the medicare system work. I do not think there is any quarrel whatsoever with the statement I am about to make: every party in this House for many years has accepted the need for medicare for our people on a universal basis. If all parties accept this principle then surely the government should pay us the compliment of listening to our attempts to try to help it get at these escalating costs which are rising so fast that they are endangering the social welfare schemes.
In view of the accumulated experience in this type of legislation having to do with delivery of health services of many members on this side of the House, surely the government has a duty to listen to some of their proposals in this debate. If I may go back to February 17 when I spoke on the original motion to send this bill to committee, I would like to remind hon. members that the question of universal health services is not new in North America. I happen to have been one of the two who in 1936, 40 years ago, moved a motion calling for prepaid medical and hospital services in Saskatchewan. Eventually Saskatchewan got them; in 1946 it got hospitalization and in 1960 prepaid medical care. So I have some experience in this matter.
I sat in a cabinet that saw the mistakes that had been made in the United Kingdom when they brought in their hospital and medical care schemes, and which saw the mistakes made by a very sincere government in Saskatchewan when it brought in its hospital care scheme. So we set up a royal commission, with the other man who was with me in 1936 in moving that the Conservative party of Saskatchewan support pre-paid medical and hospitalization services, Mr. Hall, as commissioner, to propose a series of steps that would move forward more rapidly the concept of a universal medical care scheme in Canada in addition to hospitalization, a move designed to avoid the mistakes of uncontrolled costs both of hospitalization and medicare.
I do not quarrel with the sincerity of the Liberal government when it says it believes in medicare. I accept that. But what I do question is its sincerity in not listening to those of us who have fought the battle much longer than they for these universal schemes and who are now trying to save these schemes. We must listen to arguments from
Medical Care Act
the financial side that if costs continue to rise these schemes will be destroyed.
Having made that opening point, namely, that we are not here to scuttle the medicare scheme but that we of the opposition are trying to help the government save it, let me go back to the games the hon. member from New Brunswick referred to which politicians play. In spite of the fact that the Liberal party, in opposition from 1957 to 1963, fought like tigers ad infinitum-because there was no closure in those days-against all forms of co-operative enterprise between the federal government and the provinces, when finally they were elected as a minority government in 1963, and again in 1965, they encouraged the provinces to opt out of joint enterprises that the federal government had embarked on with the provinces during the years 1957-1963. They were the great supporters of allowing the provinces to opt out of co-operative schemes.
Then in the election of 1968 we suddenly found the Liberal party advocating cooperation of government and the provinces on medicare, with the federal government providing 50 per cent of the cost. In effect, the pressure of offering 50 per cent of the cost to the provinces forced the provinces to come into the scheme, but long before they had built up the infrastructure required to keep the cost of such a universal scheme down. Everyone remembers the protests of the province of Ontario, and today the province of Ontario is paying a heavy price for having been forced into this scheme. Now eight years later the very party that forms the Government of Canada, which was once against co-operative enterprises but which turned around in 1968 and literally forced, by economic pressure, the provinces to come into its scheme, with no financial control mechanism provided for, is deliberately opting out of its own scheme into which it forced the provinces to enter.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
May I thank Your Honour for pointing out the preposterous point brought up by the hon. member. He mentioned hospitalization. There is no question that the federal government, under the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), took the lead in asking all provinces to join together in a hospitalization plan on a co-operative basis, and that is what the hon. member referred to in his quotation.
Let me repeat what I said. With the pressure of the federal government's offering a 50 per cent contribution to medicare, any province literally had to join with the scheme for political reasons. But they joined the scheme

March 15, 1976
Medical Care Act
without proper preparation of the infrastructure to keep costs under some form of control.
It is on the question of control that I want once again, as we move into the final hours of this closure debate, to plead with the government when the bill gets to committee to consider the proposals I am making as positive proposals that would get it out of its problems. All parties-I should speak only for the official opposition-want to do what we can to stop this ever-rising expenditure by governments which is breaking the country. This bill is legislating that the increase this year will not be stopped but will only be allowed to rise by 13 per cent. That amount of increase is being legislated.
We are not proposing that the increase be cut to zero. What we are asking is that the government get at the basic causes of rising costs. The fact is that these schemes are universal, but insufficient care is taken to see that the schemes are not abused. Many people ask me whether I have any positive evidence, if incentive is provided not to abuse universal programs, that the people will respond. I do have examples, Mr. Speaker, and I will quote just one in the city of Saskatoon.
In Saskatoon there is a labour union, small in number, comprising about 200 members. Following completion of negotiations on wages and working conditions one of the union members in the negotiating team proposed that they discuss, without controversy being raised, the idea that the sick leave that the city granted these workers amounting to 18 days a year be banked, to the benefit of the city. If there were 20 sick leave days a year in a union contract, over a 40-45 year life of a contract an individual would have a right to 800 or 900 days of sick leave. Human nature being what it is, if the sick leave were 18 or 20 days a year many workers would take the full amount. This particular union had a record of about 14 or 15 days of sick leave per person per year, which meant that the city had to pay the full wages of the replacement for that person who was sick according to the contract.
When this particular union's negotiator took this into the discussion without prejudicing the previous agreement, management immediately responded and said that if they would work and set up a bank of days the city would be prepared to give a full year of days in that bank that would be paid to the person in cash, either the year before the person quit or on the day the person quit. This meant that the average 14 or 15 days sick leave per man per year dropped to about half a day per man per year. This now meant that when a man went out on Saturday night and still had a headache on Monday morning he would go to work because he knew that by staying away the amount in the sick-day bank would be reduced quite rapidly for him on retirement. Obviously the city was a big gainer in that situation. The city gained some 14 or 15 days per person of free labour because of the many advantages in the proposal. I will give another example of a similar nature.
I know there are sick leave arrangements in the civil service here in Ottawa. I am simply pointing out the principle that there is a place in these universal schemes for the individual, for his own benefit and that of his family, not to abuse the schemes any more than he or she

must. This meets the problem in respect of the doctors and others, with those who take the attitude that the services are free and they should be used whether or not they are needed.
In my remarks on February 17 I said that if the government is really serious about meeting social services fixed costs now, which make up 80 per cent of the total amount of money this parliament spends each year, and if it wanted seriously to do something about combining hospitalization, medical care, old age pensions, and some day, I hope, accident insurance also, into one package, it could do so. Each individual would pay at the actuarial rates established by the experts who prepare these things.
Out of this amount approximately one third would be paid in for those who are chronically ill, for those who are chronically unemployed and those who are unable to help themselves. This is a social responsibility of all of us. The balance would go into an individual account, which is electronically possible now although it was not possible 20 years ago. Every time an individual went to hospital he or she would know that their costs would be paid. If they went to the doctor they would know that their costs would be paid. Every time an individual was unemployed he would know that his costs would be paid. He would know that every time he had an accident he would be looked after.
The scheme would be on a universal basis. The individual would know that if he drew it all out and went beyond a certain amount he would receive only the minimum amount as his old age pension. He would know that if he used the plan just the average amount, if he visited a doctor just the average amount, or was unemployed the average amount, and had an average number of accidents, the amount that would accumulate at the present interest rates and the present contribution rates would represent an additional $400 or $500 in his pension at age 65.
In such a case I think the situation would be similar to that in respect of the union I mentioned in Saskatoon. A person would be willing as an individual to protect himself and his family, and he would make it very difficult for any doctor to get him into hospital for a cut finger or any other similar ailment. All of a sudden there would be a great pressure for the doctors to restore home visits and be paid for them, which is not always the case now. All the devices would be used in an effort to keep down the costs. That individual would be careful about every expenditure. It has been estimated that about 50 per cent or 60 per cent of these total costs would disappear if individuals enforced their own use of the plan. So instead of talking about spending $100 million or $300 million more a year, which worries the finance minister now, let us look at a positive approach by which we could save billions of dollars a year through the use of a package approach.
I put forward this proposal not because it is new but because it has been around and never tried. It has been checked actuarially in the Clark Report of 1959-62.1 simply say that politicians have some responsibility to their electors and that they should look at information that is already available. With the higher rates of contribution to the plans, the higher use of these plans and the higher the cost of all these services, we should look for an idea of how we could reduce these items and provide an increased old
March 15, 1976

age pension by the introduction of this sort of a package deal. Once again, as I say, I do not have the machinery to do the calculation myself. The calculation could be made in a few months with the machinery the government has at its disposal.
These universal schemes would be combined and the people would pay a fee, a portion of which would go for the social needs of all of us and the balance would be placed in an individual account. I know this is done in respect of the operation of the Canadian Wheat Board. The sales of each individual farmer can be accounted for there. If his account number is punched the computer can tell the number of bushels of wheat, the number of bushels of barley, and the number of bushels of oats, of every grade, and the price in respect of every Canadian Wheat Board transaction made by the farmer.
This is done in respect of social security in the United States. It is done in many cases. I think that if a man were told he could use the excess in his account to increase his old age pension there would be a tremendous individual incentive to use these schemes only as a person's health demanded.
Having said all that, I know there will be thousands of cases where through no fault of the individual all the benefits will be used and therefore there will not be any increased amount in the old age pension under this proposal. I also know there will be a certain number of people, no matter what inducement is placed before them, who will abuse every plan that is put before them because this is their nature. But I would think between 60 per cent and 80 per cent of the people in a community of 22 million or 23 million people like Canada would respond to an individual incentive.
This is very different from the type of situation we have now with a negative deterrent. I spoke rather sternly a month ago on the evils of a single individual negative deterrent. I pointed out that when you put on a deterrent fee for hospital or medical use you punish the sick, the person who is the last one who should be punished.
I pointed out that where the individual deterrent had been tried on an individual basis the political party that tried it ended up by being defeated. I warned the politicians on the government side that by the universal deterrent they are putting in here, without making any effort to get at the basic causes of the rising inflationary cost push, which will simply put up the ceiling which might rise to 13 per cent, and the effect of putting a brake on these things that have gone out of control, will result in the punishment of only one person, the sick person, and there will be widespread revulsion against this.
Also you have the pressure to face that the country simply cannot stand paying $16 billion, $18 billion or $20 billion a year in these open-ended accounts. We know it is a major cause of the inflation we are suffering today, and we know it is destroying people who are trying to earn enough and save enough to have old age security of their own. We know we have to stop this inflation. I am simply pointing out in a positive and constructive sort of way that there is an alternative.
Medical Care Act
I for one do not mind voting for the motion of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) in which he suggests that we give this bill a six months hoist and let the government have time to think about this idea.
I am sure that among the elected representatives on the opposite side there must be some who are willing to challenge the control that senior members of the civil service have over them. The civil service mandarins have consistently tried for over 30 years to build up a system of controls and regulations in Canada. They think that as long as they hand over the patronage to the politicians they should have the right to run this country on a controlled system. Here they have a chance now in the Liberal party, even if only a few of them stand up in caucus, to say they should take a look at this proposal and not just turn it down and accuse the opposition of obstructionism because they have talked on a matter as important as this for 13 days. The opposition would stop here as of now.
I am not entirely in agreement with those on my left. I have read their speeches and I have a feeling they want all the money we need to handle all these social services, including medicare. I read one statement to the effect that Ontario is trying to save $50 million by closing down some hospitals. That is all part of the program that will be spread across the country soon. There will have to be restrictions. The inference in that statement is: "What is $50 million? Canada is a rich country." I am simply saying that that attitude must also be controlled. But I do not see members of the NDP opposing my proposal. God knows, I have never questioned their sincerity on the need for medicare; let them not question ours when we talk about practical ways to provide positive individual incentives and not to abuse these schemes.
I have hammered in this point as hard as I can, not only to save billions of dollars for the people who go into these schemes but to save the schemes themselves. I know from the experience in Great Britain and some of the countries in Europe, and now in North America, that even though we have been rich countries we are coming to the state where people are getting fed up to the teeth with this ever climbing tax load and the knowledge that all their savings are being wiped out by inflation. One of the causes is this ever increasing cost of government, the interest rates, and so on.
I would hate to see the antagonism of the people rise to the point where they would support policies by any government to slash these schemes and throw them aside. But I do believe that personal incentive, if accepted by the provinces and the federal government with their joint program, has great leverage and that we should save these schemes and reduce the expenses eventually and then have an automatic control mechanism which would not allow them to get out of hand in the future.
I want to conclude by a simple plea to the government members. This is not a political game to some of us. It is something that is a lifelong objective of trying to provide certain minimum fundamental means to the people that the country can afford, such as food, shelter, and medicare, which I think rank as the first three. People in all parties have fought in their legislature and in their parliament for these objectives. I and all those who are listening to me certainly do not want to see antagonism rising against

March 15, 1976
Medical Care Act
these heavy expenditures resulting in reactionary and negative policies of putting on a ceiling or brake, because I know from bitter experience that when you put on these deterrents it is always the sick person who suffers. The smart guys always know how to get around it.
Therefore I am pleading for all I am worth-I do not have much weight, I know-for somebody in the Liberal party to stand up in their caucus, and hopefully in their cabinet, and say, "Let us take a look at it. We are tired of being run by a group of civil servants who have been consistently wrong for 30 years on the monetary policy, the fiscal policy, and the trade policy, and about this business of putting on services on a universal basis without having a built in individual incentive to make them work."
I would like to see the red blood corpuscles of people who sit on the government benches rise up and make them speak out, because it has happened in other parties and it has had effect on the cabinet. They have been trying to prove in the uproar of the last two weeks that they can stand firm against the claim of the opposition that something improper is going on, but they will stand firm only so long as the caucus stands firm behind them.
The appalling thing we are witnessing here, not only in the episode of the judges, but in the Hamilton harbour case, the question of the SIU, the Austin case and all the rest of them, is that many people on the government benches do not ever think they are doing wrong. Here I am giving them a chance on something that has nothing to do with the patronage system which they seem to worship so much; here is a chance in the field of social welfare to help save it by getting at the basic costs and letting the individual provide the discipline. If you put your faith in the great majority of people, I do not think the individual Canadian will let us down. I hope the government will give this consideration instead of looking at it as a game, applying closure and shutting off the debate.

There were some labour and farmer and socialist groups in various parts of the country which were the forerunners of our movement, but I think that any objective student of history, including any of us, would have to agree that the progressive element in Canadian politics was represented by what the Liberal convention fought and stood for in 1919.
In particular I should like modern-day Liberals-the few older ones who are around may have seen this book before but I suspect some of the younger ones did not know of its existence-to read Mr. Mackenzie King's speech in introducing the labour and social policy resolution that was passed at that convention. Some of the things that are in it we surely should have had a long time before that. Some of the things in it were already common practice in democratic countries of western Europe and some other parts of the world, but they were not yet here in Canada so the Liberal party took its stand for a whole host of progressive measures in the social and labour fields.
It is true that if you read through this document you will find a lot of hoopla in it, though not quite as lively as the hoopla of modern conventions. You will find a lot of condemning of the government in power, and a lot of passing the buck and all of that. But I say quite categorically, Mr. Speaker, that the commitment the Liberals made in 1919 to try to move this country forward was quite noteworthy.
Included in the list of things that the Liberal party committed itself to in 1919, as set out in the resolution moved by Mackenzie King, was a commitment to old age pensions, unemployment insurance, and health insurance. One might have hoped, of course, that since that party got into power a couple of years later it would not have taken long until those objectives were realized. But even the progressive Liberals of the 1920's were pretty slow moving. It actually took more than 40 years to get the Liberals to come through with all the things they had promised in that great convention of 1919.
During those 40 years or more there had to be an awful lot of prodding from this side of the House. Our forerunners in the persons of Mr. Woodsworth, Miss Agnes Mac-Phail and Mr. Heaps had to get here. The C.C.F. had to come along, and then the NDP, to prod all these things. I think it is fair to suggest that over those 40 or 50 years the Liberal party did move in the direction of social legislation for the good of Canada.

It was 1926 before the first of the commitments was brought into effect, namely, old age pensions, and the history of that is pretty well known. It was a minority parliament in which there had been no mention in the throne speech that there would be old age pensions when Mr. Woodsworth and his friends wrote letters to all the parties and called for their
March 15, 1976

stand on that issue. They got from Mr. King a promise that old age pensions would be introduced in that parliament. Mr. King had to be pressed considerably even after that, but the bill was introduced in that short minority parliament. Although the bill got passed by this House it was defeated in the other place.
There followed an election, and after that election Mr. King brought the bill back again so that by the end of 1926 or the beginning of 1927 we did have a start on an old age pension system. Old age pensions are not the subject tonight so I shall not take time to describe what that pension was like and the long battle to get it improved. The point is that it took from 1919 to 1926 or 1927 to get the first of these items implemented.
The second item was unemployment insurance. Again we had a promise, a commitment of the great Liberal Party of Canada in its great convention of 1919. So what year was unemployment insurance passed? In 1940, 21 years later, coming into effect in 1941.
For health insurance the struggle was long and almost endless. I remember about 1947 or 1948 when there were rumours around that Mr. King, who was getting near the end of his time as prime minister-was getting near the end of his time in fact-had decided that before he finished he wanted to put health insurance on the statute books. I remember the excitement here one day when word got around that Mr. King would make a statement on motions in the House that afternoon and it would concern health. Some of us were naive enough to think that at long last, in 1948, we were going to get the health insurance that had been promised in 1919. That is not what we got, Mr. Speaker. We got instead the announcement of the hospital grants that the federal government was prepared to make to the provinces. There was no provision in this at all for medical care, but there was the beginning of money to assist the provinces in the building of hospitals.
I remember very well hearing Mr. King say in 1948, all those years after 1919, that we could not do these things overnight, that there was no point in talking about hospital insurance or medical care insurance until the infrastructure-I do not think he used that word because we did not use it in 1948-until all the equipment and buildings were ready and enough doctors had been trained. So in 1948 the notion that we were going to get health insurance proved to be false. It was actually 1957 before the Liberals finally brought in the first act having to do with hospitalization.
Even that act had in it a provision that required a majority of the provinces to come in before it would be effective. It was left to the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) to modify that act when his party came into power so that the provinces could come into the hospitalization legislation one by one.
We had to go all the way to the middle 1960's, to the years when Lester Pearson was prime minister, before the Medical Care Act was finally passed. We waited a long time, from the initial Liberal promise of 1919 until the middle 1960's, to get the Liberal party to implement the glowing promises it had made to Canada. We waited some 45 or 46 years. At least they were moving-

My hon. friend says they were creeping. At least they were creeping in the right direction.
In all these discussions about pensions, unemployment insurance, and later about hospitalization and medical care it was established that if the programs were to be of value to the people of Canada they had to be equally available across the country. The idea of co-operation with the provinces is spelled out in the resolution passed by the national Liberal convention of 1919. The Liberals of that day accepted the need for co-operation between Ottawa and the provinces and that schemes had to be introduced which would make social services like pensions, unemployment insurance, hospitalization, and medical care equally available to all right across the country.
Having been present in the House during the last six years of the prime ministership of Mackenzie King and having been a member during the prime ministerships of Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Pearson, I felt that there was a certain tendency on the part of the Liberal party, especially on Mr. Pearson's part, to implement the social commitment which had been made in 1919. As a result we saw improvements in old age pensions; the government introduced the Canada Pension Plan, and we saw improved unemployment insurance. We were given a type of improved hospitalization program, and then we saw the provision for medical care.
My complaint, which I have made previously and which I repeat this evening, is that the modern-day Liberal party under the leadership of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is reversing that long Liberal trend.
