What an interruption! It shows that the members on the Liberal side do not know what they are doing. The advantage of our present hospital and medical care scheme is that the service is more or less the same in all parts of Canada. If the federal government's share of what provinces must pay to provide medical care and hospitalization goes down, the provinces will have either to cut back services, impose deterrent fees or introduce special charges. When that day comes you will see better service at less cost, in some provinces, and poorer service at a higher cost in others.
The great party across the way talks of national unity. Well, it is destroying national unity where it hurts. When you talk of national unity you do not talk just about language. National unity also counts in terms of health and in terms of the pocket book. As I say, what bothers me is that for 40 years the Liberals seemed to be moving in the right direction. But these characters on the other side who now call themselves Liberals are prepared to send it all down the drain. All the arguments they have been trying to give us in the last few days, and again tonight, about there being more dollars in the next few years do not get away from the fact that they are trying to provide for a lesser share to be paid by the federal government.
There are other schemes coming along like a guaranteed annual income or a new social security system, again on a shared basis. I cannot blame the provinces for being very suspicious about these new shared programs. In the first place, they are put to them in a way that attracts them. It invites the provinces to come in. When they have the experience that down the line somewhere the federal share is reduced, it can only make the provinces leery.
There are some programs such as the old age security that so far we have been able to maintain at the same level right across Canada. The guaranteed income supplement is

also at the same level right across Canada. However, already, because the federal government has not raised old age security to the amount it ought to be raised and because it has let down the old age pensioners, governments like those in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and some others have had to come in with special supplements. These supplements vary from province to province. Therefore right today an amount that a pensioner is able to get if he has nothing else varies considerably from province to province. In my book that is not national unity.
These characters across the way, these hon. members who comprise the governing party, are destroying the very basis of national unity. They are selling out the very thing for which their party stood and worked for so many years, even if it took a lot of prodding to get them to do it.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. Victor Railton (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to follow the very eminent member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who had so much misinformation for this House, particularly from the standpoint of doctors, with respect to Bill C-73 and Bill C-68 which he did not seem able to separate.
Over this past week end I have been reading the speeches of different members. I have also read the remarks made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). I tried to get the ideas being presented here about health care and Bill C-68 into my head. I have gone over a lot of speeches. The minister has been making statements which are very consistent and easy to understand. He has emphasized several things.
First, medicare and hospital care costs, exclusive of extra benefits which some provinces have initiated, have risen by 22.5 per cent last year, will rise 20 per cent this year, and will again rise 18 per cent next year. I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is listening.
Second, for several years negotiations with the provinces about modifications of our cost-sharing arrangements have been unsuccessful in spite of valiant efforts of the Liberal-federal government-I was going to say Liberal government, it is liberal-and constant demonstration of fair treatment both to have and have-not provinces. That is a new phrase, have and have-not. Just like the countries of the world, the provinces are listed much the same. The federal government pays the biggest share in all of these schemes and the amount varies from 54 per cent to 74 per cent, never in any case below 50 per cent.

March 15, 1976
Medical Care Act
Third, starting with the budget of June, 1975, and culminating in Bill C-68, the government has proposed to put ceilings on the increase of annual contributions from Ottawa to the provinces. All it is doing is putting ceilings on the contributions. It is not decreasing them. These increases are 13 per cent, 10 per cent, and possibly 8 per cent in the third year but I think the minister has relented and made the last figure 10 per cent and it is likely to continue to be 10 per cent for a year or two thereafter- there is a likelihood that this will continue for five years.
There is one more point. The federal government, as required by law, is serving notice on the provinces that it will terminate and replace existing agreements under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. This allows five years for new agreements to be drawn up, plenty of time in which to review not only cost-sharing but the whole question of possible changes in the health care delivery system.
Looking over the speeches made in the House it is almost incredible how plain statements, so logically presented, were so generally misunderstood or, should I say, so universally misrepresented by all members speaking from the opposition side.
This bill has consumed a vast number of hours during the present session. Too much time has been spent already on this one piece of legislation. I heartily congratulate the government House leader for putting forward the motion which sets limits on further debate. He could not pursue any other course without being unmindful of the government's duty to the people.
It is well known that there is an adequate number of general hospital beds in Canada per capita. In fact we have more beds per capita than they have in the United States or in the United Kingdom. Our greatest need in the matter of beds is for long-stay patients who may be convalescing from acute conditions or for chronically ill patients requiring continuing or permanent hospital care. The federal government for some years has been exploring with the provinces the possible extension of hospital insurance programs to include lower levels of institutional care. This would require the provinces shifting some of the emphasis from expensive acute services to less costly but equally acceptable alternatives. All this could be tidied up before the end of the next five years.
Most members who spoke for the NDP charged that the federal government was reducing its contribution. This is contrary to the facts. There will not be a reduction of services or any need for provinces to increase taxation above levels previously envisaged. Every province could still enjoy the present level of good medical care. Nowhere will there be any reduction in medical research because the rate of escalated contributions would always be held above the inflationary index.

speechtext: Can you keep a straight face and say that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those pious, rather hypocritical expressions of melancholy and cries that the provinces were being abandoned are completely unfounded. Most of those speakers-and I am referring now to members of the

New Democratic Party-felt there was no need to economise or cut frills. Some advocated complete disregard for spiralling costs. In fact they counselled us to leave things exactly as they are, no matter what the cost. How impractical can you be?
The Progressive Conservatives, on the other hand-and there were plenty of good speeches made over there-said the government had acted unilaterally without giving warning to the provinces. The minister has shown how false this accusation really is. He was, as usual, called arrogant-a favourite opposition description of any courageous move on the part of the government.
Conservative spokesmen also asked, "Why bring in Bill C-68; surely the anti-inflation controls under C-73 will be enough to look after increasing costs?" The crux of the matter is that negotiations must be completed in the next five years and agreement achieved. Given any kind of co-operation, this question should have been settled already.
Our worthy opponents opposite even blame the federal government for the inept "bull-in-the-china-shop" type of hospital closures recently seen in Ontario. If this happened to be the object of Frank Miller's or Bill Davis' ploy, it certainly backfired. These inept confrontations between the Ontario department of health and the unfortunate hospitals which have been closed down only increased the difficulties of Ontario's hospitalization program.
It is very hard to see how the complete closure of hospitals such as the Doctors' Hospital, the Clinton Hospital, and the Paris Hospital can save money for anybody. First, the hospital staff becomes unemployed. Next, the hospital buildings must be maintained even if they are not used. Third, the patients must be moved to other hospitals where they will be cared for at greater expense. In my opinion it would have been much better had there been some reduction in the over-all bed establishment at all Ontario hospitals. At the same time the number of beds reserved for patients suffering from acute conditions could have been reduced and other wards could have been set aside and used by convalescent patients. As I mentioned before, these "lower level" beds could still serve the community well, though in some cases the status, medically, of the community hospital of necessity would have to be lowered.
We have been criticized incorrectly because of this interpretation. It has been said that the federal government has instituted cuts whose effects would be to reduce health care services. In fact, as explained earlier, the government has simply put ceilings on annual increases in its contributions. These are still well above the inflationary rate. The whole subject has received a great deal of study and it is well known that these ceilings will not jeopardize the present program. Nevertheless it is imperative that both sides reach an agreement.
Our mortality rate, our medicare and hospitalization systems, have been compared to those of foreign countries. We realize that a health delivery system enjoys continuance of the status quo, but it is not sacrosanct. People in Canada rather like our present system which allows doctors to carry on private practices. There is no doubt that the level of medical care in Canada in doctors' offices is much superior to that in the United Kingdom. It is the
March 15, 1976

hospitals, though, which are at the centre of our medical care system.
Victims of drug overdoses, drunks, psychologically upset families, and people hurt in car accidents crowd into our hospital emergency wards at night and especially on week ends. The hospital has become over-used. This is due partly to pressure from people frequenting the emergency facilities and sometimes to over-servicing by thoughtless doctors. Only in hospitals can major operations be performed.
It has become clear that doctors cannot do house calls and still see all the people who crowd into their offices or even into outpatient departments. Even though there is one doctor for every 900 people in Canada some people feel there is an under-supply of medical care. It is quite possible that the present dilemma can only be solved by using a new approach to health care delivery systems.
When one considers that many day-to-day patient complaints are minor, it would seem that a highly educated professional man is not required to use his knowledge and skill very often. It has been contended that many patients coming into outpatient departments or even into doctors' offices could be seen primarily by a paramedical assistant in the OPD or in the home. Following that, only a small percentage would need to see a doctor. However, if this plan were to be adopted the excellence of treatment would inevitably deteriorate. The experienced, well trained physician can quickly tell how serious a case is, whereas a paramedic might understandably misjudge the situation.
In spite of this, if we are to give universally free care to all, we may be forced to reorganize our system and still wisely make use of our medical brains. With a different type of organization we could certainly make use of nurse practitioners, medics, supertrained orderlies and operating room assistants. The whole system would have to be overhauled and organized for efficiency and reduced expense. However, the rising salaries of other levels of medical care personnel make one wonder whether this would really lead to a reduction in costs.
At the present time there have been great changes in hospital administration. About 25 years ago most hospital funds were concentrated on providing care and treatment to the patient. Now, because of our accreditation program, mention of which was made earlier in the debate, and because of the need for uniformity of high level treatment, efficiency experts have become hospital administrators and a great deal of money has had to be spent on documentation. This is always the trouble in trying to devise efficient systems-sometimes the patient suffers, though the statistics look good.
There is no doubt that central district hospitals looking after a large number of specialties are the most efficient way to care for the sick. Satellite hospitals could be built or continue to be used in the surrounding areas. Their work of necessity would be at a lower level. Where a hospital has been built and possesses enough land some of these convalescent, chronic and extended care buildings could very advantageously be built very close to the original acute hospital. There is what we are trying to do in my own constituency of Welland where the board was farsighted enough to build the hospital on between 15 and 20
Medical Care Act
acres of land. In these district hospitals a very well-endowed intensive care unit is a necessity and all the diagnostic tools must be available.
I feel sometimes that the promotion of private laboratories was a mistake. There has recently been a great deal of suspicion about the financial probity of some of these private laboratories. Ideally, all x-ray examinations and laboratory examinations would be done in the hospital or under hospital supervision, and where this does not take place private institutions have sometimes lent themselves to unscrupulous ordering of total body x-rays and total laboratory examinations which are not required. This increases the private institution's income, and for this reason alone hospital supervision should be mandatory.
In my speech, except perhaps for the last few remarks, I have tried to stay fairly close to Bill C-68, which I hope will pass quickly. I think it has been misunderstood and I am sure it has been wilfully misinterpreted. However, I think that not only must we examine suggestions for improved financing but we must allow for change in our medical care and hospital care systems. This evolution has to proceed constantly as we learn new methods.
On February 11 last the Minister of National Health and Welfare wrote a letter to the editor of the Globe and Mail in Toronto and very explicitly drew his attention to disparaging references about the national medical care program made in his paper. The minister said that from the editorial it would seem that experience of medicare has been so severe that the federal government is "trying to dump it totally on the provinces". The minister continued:
I find this somewhat ironical since I have just written a letter to the Editor of the Ottawa Journal who ... had accused me of totally backing down to the provinces and abandoning our efforts to restrain the rate of cost increase. Both points of view are, of course, totally erroneous.
That is the point I have been trying to make in my speech. The minister went on to say that he felt that the editorial writer had presented his data in a most misleading fashion. Further on the minister went on to say this: What your editorial writer does not point out is that in 1967-68 the health-related expenditures, which in 1975-76 amounted to approximately 30 per cent of the provincial budget, took up 31 per cent of the provincial budget. He perhaps overlooked the fact that the Ontario Hospital Services Commission had its own budget, separate from the Ministry of Health, in those days. To the $359 million shown in the Ministry's 1967-68 budget one has to add $412 million from the OHSC budget to compare with 1975-76. Also, before medicare a number of provincial departments had medical expenditures which, following medicare, were put into one pot and shown subsequently in the health department's budget. In any event the budget of the Ministry of Health today does not appear to take up any larger proportion of the current provincial budget that the health-related expenditures took up during the several pre-medicare years.
I do not intend to read the whole letter, Mr. Speaker, but I think it would be of advantage to members of the House to read it. For some reason I feel there has been a very stubborn and obtuse attempt on the part of all opposition parties in the House to misrepresent the government's policy on health care, and I deplore this. I do not see, and have never seen, why anyone in politics would misrepresent a case just for their own political gain.

for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has a tremendous amount of experience in the House, and of my hon. friend, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton). Others who have contributed to the debate have shown there are still things to be said.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Chretien) has just entered the Chamber. I remember in 1967 or 1968 he said we do not have enough money to institute the medical care act. It was postponed for a whole year. The present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), who was then the Minister of National Health and Welfare, brought in this act shortly after. It was discussed at some length in this House.
In respect of the compromises concerning the situation we are in, together with the galloping expenses of health care and so on, it is interesting to note that a system was already in operation in the province of Ontario under the premier of that day, Mr. Robarts. It is interesting to note that 80 per cent of the people of the province of Ontario were covered through one insurance scheme or another. Prior to that the plan was run by the Ontario Physicians Services. The administration costs, if I remember correctly, were around 2 per cent. A fine new building was built, and at the time it was closed there was a reserve fund.
Today, out of the $7 fee a physician receives for his service, the government takes 10 per cent. No one really knows what are the administrative costs. One thing we do know is that every doctor is humbugged by papers and papers and by bureaucracy and bureaucracy, until a third of his time is spent filling out papers when he should be devoting that time to his patients. This is bureaucracy.
When Mr. Robarts introduced a health care bill in the province of Ontario to cover the 25 per cent of the population in that province who had some problems in meeting their medical bills he introduced a sliding scale by which those who had a certain income would make no payments, those in another income scale would make a payment of a certain percentage, and those in another income scale would have to pay the whole premium. This was all underwritten by the insurance companies. This plan was carried much more cheaply than the national scheme is carried today.
When the federal government introduced the national medical care bill it still taxed the people of the province of Ontario. That province was forced into the medical care plan, after the federal government had received some $125 million from the province of Ontario which was paid into the national medical care plan.
There is no way the federal government can escape the responsibility for the national medical care bill. The federal government forced this on the provinces whether or not they liked it, because the provinces were taxed for it in any event.
I was interested in the speech made by my young friend from Gloucester when he spoke about the doctors so kindly. Let me tell him from my lengthy experience that there is no way the doctors can be separated from the hospital or health care scheme. They work together. The hon. member made a very good speech, but he was completely wrong when he said we could separate the fields. I

should like to tell the hon. member that young doctors, after they have been working for three or four years, expect a raise. At that time they usually can expect to have more patients and therefore have a higher income, but under the anti-inflation bill they are limited to an increase of $2,400. There is no way the hon. member can equate that with an increase of 13 per cent.

In 1969 it was pointed out in this House by the then minister of national health and welfare that the rising costs were becoming a considerable factor. He pointed this out dramatically. Although he mentioned that it may be difficult to carry out the plan he said there were three ways in which it could be done. He mentioned a deterrent fee. Let me say to everybody in this House that if there was any reason for bringing in a national medical care bill it was so that the poor could obtain the necessary care. A deterrent fee works directly against that purpose.
We heard in 1969 that we would be in trouble. The various ministers of national health and welfare in this House and the ministers of health for the provinces have had seven years in which to find ways and means to face the problem of the rising costs. I want to ask what they have done. They have had closed meetings and other meetings. What have we heard? If one looks at Hansard one can see the replies to the questions that have been asked. We are told that the ministers are getting together and that the problem would be dealt with, but that has gone on for the last six years. Where do we stand today? What is the situation in respect of these problems?
We are facing a situation of deteriorating health care in a country that was known world-wide for its health care plan. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all the members in this House that I, as one of the older physicians, regret this very much. In certain areas they are taking measures today which result in the reduction of the incentive to work which we used to have under the old scheme. The good relationship between the patient and the doctor is pretty well gone nowadays.

I want to ask the minister why some means and ways have not been found whereby people could be treated more cheaply. In the last seven years they have had the opportunity to work out schemes to provide by alternative methods the high cost care which now is cut off. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that it does not seem fair or right that we should pay the money we are paying to have the administration, not only at the provincial level but at the federal level, cut down on services. It is not right that some system has not been worked out so that expensive health care which they are talking about now could be provided by cheaper means and the closing of hospitals would not be necessary. What we see now shows a completely immature knowledge in a field that they are not expert enough to handle.
I watch this, Mr. Speaker, and I look at my own province, the province in which this House of Commons is located. What about the house calls that the physician used to make? I say to you, Mr. Speaker, if they want a broadcast on this I will go across Canada and speak on this issue, even if they want to talk about Quebec, Nova Scotia or Manitoba. I will talk about these provinces because I happen to know what is going on there also. So if they want to broaden the field and speak about provinces other than the province of Ontario, I will tell them about the other provinces as well as about the province in which this House of Commons is located, a province which pays 38 per cent of all the taxes in Canada. I will tell them about that province having to cut down its health schemes, having to close its hospitals. I say that when that happens there is something radically wrong with this scheme which was brought in here in 1968. That is the point I am making.
I want to say that I have some records which indicate that people can be treated more cheaply in their own homes. I refer to one specific case of two people over 90 years of age who would have been placed in treatment homes but for the fact that a doctor interested in their case said, "We will treat these people at home, if possible." He went out a distance of ten miles to make his calls and he arranged for a lady to go to the house to look after these two patients in their own home at $100 a week. Do you know what it would have cost on an average in any hospital in Ontario? It would have cost around $100 a day. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what it would have cost to have those patients in one of the treatment homes of which they
Medical Care Act
have many in Ontario which provide extended care? It would have cost $20 a day.
The government assured people they would get health care, and the minister said that there would be no lack of health care across Canada. I would like to take them to hospitals where patients are not getting good health care. I was in an institution the other day and the bells started ringing, the buzzers from patients' rooms. I asked what the heck had gone wrong because you could hardly hear yourself. I was told that four of the people on the nursing staff had been dismissed to save money. Who is suffering? It is the patient. Who is overworked? It is the nurse and the nurse's assistant. That is the type of health care people are getting.
I ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the health ministers across this country, what in the name of heavens is wrong that they cannot jointly work out a system to provide less expensive health care which would allow people to be treated in homes where they could get home care? Surely they have a home care program starting and federal moneys are paid into this program, but what type of home care is it? Under certain conditions it is very good if there is someone else in the home apart from the patient. Under that program they will send a person to the home for eight hours, which is a help, but what if that patient is alone? Why can they not provide a 24 hour service? Would it not be cheaper to provide a 24 hour service than to pay $100 a day for an active treatment bed, as well as emergency expenses, because a patient has to go through the emergency ward to get to the active treatment bed?
They are closing down hospitals, cutting down services, and at the same time patients have to be moved from the hospitals that are being closed. Ambulances have to go out farther, yet they are cutting ambulance budgets. You know what happens when that budget is cut. Someone might lose his life because instead of the ambulance reaching him in half an hour he may have to wait two hours as a result of the call system which exists across Ontario.
Here is the situation in which we find ourselves. We have a deteriorating health care scheme, which is a problem of not only this parliament but a problem which this legislation imposes through an act of this parliament on all provinces across Canada, some of which had a better scheme.
I want to say this very definitely to my friend, the hon. member for Gloucester, that the provinces which will be hurt first of all are the poor provinces such as the Atlantic provinces. He knows it, and there is no way around it.

I should also like to mention the speech of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton). He too reached into his experience in this area. A little later I shall come to the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I speak as one who is a consumer of medical care and one who is concerned about the problems the government faces in meeting the high cost and the huge sums of money that are dispensed for health care. I think it is important after
12	days of debate on this issue that we go over again what the bill is supposed to do. There seems to be a great deal of confusion, some I am sure deliberate and perhaps some innocent, about the effect of the bill.
First of all I think it should be fully understood that this is a medical care bill only; it deals with doctors' fees and medicare, but does not deal with hospitalization. I think it is important that this be made clear. The bill says that in the year beginning April 1, 1976, the increase over the previous year will be limited to 13 per cent, for the subsequent year 11 per cent, and the third year to be negotiated, but will probably be 10 per cent. These figures are the increases in the cost of medical care that will be allowed by the federal government which pays, depending on the affluence of the province, roughly 50 per cent of the total cost. I think it would be a very cruel act to bring this particular bill in to limit these costs if we were not at the same time bringing in an anti-inflation program.
The anti-inflation program, with the setting up of the board and the control on wages, and the attempt to control prices, will work, and I think it is important. Putting this
13	per cent up against what we hope will be only 8 'A per cent inflation in the first year that is covered, April 1, 1976 to April 1, 1977, and to say after that we would hope this would be down to 6 per cent or 7 per cent-say 13 per cent versus 8'A per cent or 8 per cent, or 11 per cent versus probably 6 per cent and 7 per cent and so on-I think this is an important aspect of the bill. It is being debated after

we brought in the anti-inflation program, and I think that makes the bill a much more feasible proposition. I think we have to realize that the bill also allows for special considerations where there are significant population increases.
I should like to deal with this whole subject in terms of the two opposition parties. I should like to deal first with the New Democratic Party's position, which is the same as the Conservative party's position, but obviously for different reasons. I have a very warm feeling about the NDP, and before it the CCF, and their long term approach to the need for medical care and hospital care. I feel that the period between 1919-20 when these things were first mentioned and 1966 might have been reduced considerably had there not been a third party in this country, but rather had the progressive elements in that third party been a part of the Liberal party, the party mainly in power. The time element might very well have been shortened. That does not in any way detract from their efforts made over the years to bring about this result. There has been a genuine concern by the NDP for better health care, and I think it has been justified.
This government brought in the medicare program and has made great improvements in medical care. We have allowed the cost to rise in ratio well above the combination of the gross national product and the inflation rate over the years. This has been a good thing because it was necessary to improve medical services, and an over-run of this kind was absolutely necessary.
One of the consistent themes that the NDP has used in this House on many, many issues is its constant concern about the high level of health care, social care and so on, which inevitably means increased cost. I think the big difference between that party and our party in this respect is not in our concern but rather in the fact that we are in power. We form the government and we have to be responsible; we have to impose the limit on how much can be spent.
In terms of cost sharing arrangements with the provinces there are some very serious problems. One problem is that if we offer to pay 50 per cent, and the provinces do the spending, we do not have much control over what they spend. If they spend $100 million we will have to put up 50 per cent, and if they spend $200 million we will still have to put up 50 per cent. While it was necessary to set up these cost-sharing schemes, the plan is creating some great overrun for the federal government.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-REASON FOR NOTICE TO PILOTS TO EXERCISE CAUTION WHEN FLYING OVER QUEBEC
AIR TRANSPORT-REASON FOR NOTICE TO PILOTS TO EXERCISE CAUTION WHEN FLYING OVER QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a release concerning bilingual air traffic services dated February 25, 1976, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) used the first page to state, in capital letters and underlined, that there has not been one validated incident of a near miss which could be attributed to the use of a second language. I contend that the minister and the government are playing with the lives of pilots and air passengers when they put the demands of Francophone air traffic controllers and pilots before safety. As a matter of fact I have reason to believe that even the minister's release is a concerted attempt to mislead the public and placate the vocal federal Quebec Liberal members.
I have been in consultation with the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association. They inform me that in the past 15 months they have reported 20 incidents of close calls in the air in Quebec. To Mr. W. M. McLeish, director general of civil aeronautics, these close calls involved confusion in language, and personality conflicts between French and English, yet not one of these reports has been acknowledged by either Mr. McLeish or the department. I should like to challenge the minister on his statement that not one incident has been validated; because if that is the case one wonders why the reports were not acknowledged. Furthermore, if investigations did take place, I ask the minister to make them public.
The government claims that those who object to bilingual air traffic services are too emotional. If being concerned about the safety of people is being too emotional, I plead guilty. Safety has been cast aside for political expediency. In the few short moments I have to speak I wish to touch upon the weaknesses in the government's arguments.
Though the official language of the air has been English, the government has bowed to political pressure and carried its bilingualism program into the air. This is a safety hazard unacceptable to the Canadian Air Traffic Control Association. If these two major organizations are opposed, why has the government persisted in carrying out bilingual air traffic services? It has chosen to ignore both traffic controllers and pilots in favour of vocal minority.
The minister leans heavily on the argument that certain European countries use two languages in air traffic control but ignores the fact that English is used as the international air language. He fails to explain why a second language is needed in Canada. Until a few short months ago we operated in the international language. Furthermore, the minister avoids altogether the fact that air traffic in Europe is not nearly as great as in Canada. The minister is being irresponsible in refusing to listen to reason.
Adjournment Debate
As a concerned party I have been in consultation with pilots and their association and they have expressed serious reservations about the government's seeming lack of concern about safety. Pilots operating in a busy airspace such as the Montreal vicinity cannot afford language confusion which would create dangerous gaps and uncertainties. In such a case the lives of people would be in danger, and I really wonder what the government's excuse is going to be in the event of such a terrible tragedy as an air crash.
For the record I should like to point out some of the dangers involved in the introduction of a second language into aviation, as detailed by professionals. They include, first, the elimination of some safety redundancy built into the existing system; second, added complexity and increased workload for controllers; third, additional communications on already overloaded radio frequencies; and, fourth, unilingual Francophone pilots operating in English only controlled air space. In light of these and other dangers it has now become clear that the demands of Francophone pilots have taken priority over safety. Even the Bilcom task force, which found that an overwhelming majority of the aviation community saw no need for bilingual communications, has gone unheeded.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that all the reports and documents in the world are not going to sway the government's efforts to win political support at any cost, including safety. It is a sad day when one has to run the risk of being branded as a bigot to ensure that common sense and safety prevail.
In closing, I was informed just today that Air Canada crew members, such as stewardesses, are refusing to bid for trips into Montreal because of the dangerous bilingual traffic control situation. Also, as I pointed out two weeks ago, notices had been posted at Canadian airports by the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association warning pilots to exercise extreme caution when flying into Quebec. All in all, Mr. Speaker, it is a very sad state of affairs for Canadian air travellers and crews.

May I simply conclude, Mr. Speaker, by repeating the essential concern of the Ministry of Transport with the

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-POSSIBILITY OF INCLUDING OIL PRICES WITHIN GUIDELINES
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-POSSIBILITY OF INCLUDING OIL PRICES WITHIN GUIDELINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not surprised in answer to my question of March 9 on whether Canadian crude oil prices would come under the Anti-Inflation Board that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) gave a firm no, even though the Liberal premier of Nova Scotia had recently said that it was only political expediency that kept the federal government from doing so.
In answering the second part of my question as to whether substantial increases in equalization grants to the province of Nova Scotia, as well as maintenance of the present level of oil subsidies, would continue, the minister interpreted the question to imply that I was looking for a special Nova Scotia oil price as opposed to that payable by the rest of Canadians.
We are, of course, well aware that the federal government is already equalizing oil prices across the country at lower than the world price. The minister, however, should be aware that despite this there has been a 50 per cent rise in the cost of electricity in the province of Nova Scotia in 1975. If the federal government allows a further increase of, let us say, $2 for Canadian crude oil at the wellhead after July, which would make it about $10 a barrel, then we in Nova Scotia could well see another 50 per cent increase in the cost of electricity in the province of Nova Scotia by 1977-especially when that province's long-term and exceptionally favourable contract with Imperial Oil runs out at the end of this year. That company provides 30 per cent of all the oil used in Nova Scotia.
We know that the federal government desires to push up considerably the price of Canadian crude by July in order to fulfil its policy of allowing the price of Canadian crude to tend gradually to equal the world price. This price, of course, is not a market price but is a monopoly price. Because it is a monopoly price it should not, in my opinion, be used as a criterion for the allocation of our petroleum fuel resources. Amongst other things, it sets a dangerous policy precedent.
The Canadian cabinet as well as the American government in this connection should give the plan of Professor Morris A. Adelman of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology serious consideration. He has long been an advocate of a government oil buying program, and has proposed a government purchasing agency which would control all oil imports. I recently forwarded to the finance minister an article by Professor Adelman in which he is advocating a system of sealed bids by individual oil producing countries, which would not in itself destroy the OPEC monopoly but could be a quick and effective means of bringing international oil prices down.
I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and the premier of Nova Scotia, have brought it to the attention of the government that in every

part of the province of Nova Scotia there are increasing signs of citizen anger in the form of protest meetings and more permanent protest organizations. I honestly fear that some of this pent up anger can lead to very ugly recriminations.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs at a recent provincial Liberal gathering held in Halifax was quoted as asking the provincial government officials to avoid "trying to foment anger toward Ottawa". But what can one do when people using electrical heating, pushed at them only four or five years ago as the cleanest and cheapest way to heat a home, are reported as receiving bills for two months as high as $350?
In my constituency I have widows and pensioners on low and relatively fixed incomes coming in to see me about their electrical power bills with despair on their faces, and sometimes with tears in their eyes.
We know that the per capita income figure for Nova Scotia is often quoted as 75 to 78 per cent of the Canadian average, and that is the best of any province in the Atlantic region. The latest official figures though for Glace Bay, the largest town in my constituency, reveal that it is only 54 per cent of the Canadian average. New Waterford, the next largest town, is only 48 per cent of that average, and Cape Breton County 55 per cent.
The minister is probably aware that about 55 per cent of Nova Scotia power is generated from oil, with another 30 per cent generated by coal the price of which, through Devco, is contractually tied to the present subsidized price of oil. Thus, during last year, for example, Devco's coal division showed a deficit larger by $10 to $15 million because of this arrangement. In view of this situation, and because of the heavy unemployment in Cape Breton, the Cape Breton Development Corporation should be given the money to start two new coal mines in the area, one at Lingan in the New Waterford district and the other at Donkin in the Glace Bay region, for the generation of power. One could be immediately started in 1977 and the other, with some extra effort, by 1978. We should be taking advantage of the fact that Cape Breton coal is now not only competitive with oil for thermal power production in Nova Scotia but has the added advantage of an assured supply in case of another oil embargo.
The federal government should as well, especially in the case of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, maintain in the interim a decent level of subsidies against imported oil and make additional funds available for Nova Scotia by way of equalization payments that could be earmarked for reducing the power bills of low income home owners and those special type of businesses whose power costs are a substantial part of their total costs. The provincial government on its part as a minimum concession should forgo building expensive sport complexes, and any other needless amenities in the Halifax-Dartmouth area so as to keep down electrical costs throughout the province.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-POSSIBILITY OF INCLUDING OIL PRICES WITHIN GUIDELINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been unable to find any reference in the Globe and Mail as was mentioned by the member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) in his question. However, I do understand that Premier G. A. Regan, when speaking in support of the
March 15, 1976

government's anti-inflation program during debate in the Nova Scotia House of Assembly in Halifax, did make reference to the fact that crude oil prices are outside the ambit of the Anti-Inflation Act. This is true, Mr. Speaker, simply because petroleum prices were already subject to control under the Petroleum Administration Act when the antiinflation program was introduced.
The appropriate level of petroleum prices has been the subject of much debate in this House, at federal-provincial conferences, and by most Canadians over the past several years. They have been and continue to be subject to control under the Petroleum Administration Act. The desire for low prices must be balanced against the need to ensure adequate supplies. The provisions for oil compensation payments, which in the coming fiscal year (1976-77) are estimated to be $1.41 billion, are a unique effort to provide that balance. These controls are consistent with the antiinflation program, and it appears inappropriate to subject petroleum to two controls where one is sufficient.
I might add that among the intended changes in the anti-inflation guidelines announced one week ago, the relationship between the guidelines and the Petroleum Administration Act is being tightened to ensure that prices for petroleum products will clearly be subject to one or the other act. Crude oil prices are already subject to control under the Petroleum Administration Act, and there is neither the need nor intention to bring them specifically under the anti-inflation guidelines.

subtopic: FINANCE-EFFECT OF RAISING BANK INTEREST RATE
FINANCE-EFFECT OF RAISING BANK INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question was raised on March 8 when I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) about the recently announced increase in the bank rate. I also asked him whether he would indicate what impact he felt this increase would have on mortgage interest rates in Canada and the cost of borrowing for the average Canadian, and whether he would indicate what was the purpose of the increase in the bank rate.
In general the minister gave a most unsatisfactory answer, and I believe there is no alternative but to face the fact that we are heading for a credit crunch in this country. I believe it is necessary for the minister to bring in a new budget now, not in May. I notice that in commenting in committee, to the press, and also in the House, he has got into the habit of saying he cannot make any observation concerning various economic matters as it is a budgetary point and he feels the answer should be delayed until the budget. That is just a stall. The nation deserves answers to some of the critical questions now before us.
I refer to questions such as why should we be literally in first place among the western industrialized nations so far as our bank rate is concerned? In fact, Mr. Speaker, there is no other country in the world at the present time with a higher rate than our present bank rate, with the exception of Brazil. I point out that in Britain, which most people think is in serious shape, its bank rate has not risen above 9 per cent, where it is at the present time. Italy, whose central bank is generally regarded to be one of the weakest of the industrialized nations-in fact that nation was close
Adjournment Debate
to bankruptcy last year-got through its dilemma without raising its bank rate beyond 8 per cent.
In short, Canadians deserve some answers from the minister. For example, why should we have a Canadian prime rate of 1014 per cent at the present time, when the American prime rate is 6 3A per cent? On December 31 the prime rate in the United States was 714 per cent but it has gone down at least half a point since the end of the year. The Canadian prime rate at that time was 9 3A per cent but has gone up half a point since then.
I could cite various examples of U.S. bond rates, treasury bills, and various other debt obligations carrying interest coupons at the present time of 3 per cent, even 4 per cent, lower than those in Canada. One of the contributing factors to high interest rates in Canada is the high rate of government spending. I believe that when the government talks of restraint it is simply misleading the Canadian public. There has been no restraint evidenced by the government to date. In fact, appearing before the finance, trade and economic affairs committee last Tuesday, the Minister of Finance finally broke down and admitted that the cash drain or deficit in Canada, so far as the federal government is concerned, will be $5.5 to $6 billion in the current year. I asked him what he anticipated to be the drain in the coming fiscal year, 1977, and he startled me, frankly, by saying it would be something like that, though it was a budgetary matter and he would not be specific. In short, Mr. Speaker, in two years we will have a drain in this nation of between $11 billion and $12 billion, and this is one of the factors causing the increase in our bank rate.
Second, I would point out the impact of the increase. How many people realize, for example, that in the fiscal year 1970 the total interest in annual amortization cost to the federal government of our national debt was $1.7 billion? In the estimates now before us for 1977 the cost has gone up to 4,641,000,000. That is an increase of 271 per cent in a period of seven years. This is the interest load the government is inflicting upon the Canadian people either through the higher rate structure or increase of debt.
Again this impact is felt by the average home owner in this country. I pointed out that in the United States the rate is about three percentage points below ours. People there are able to write off their interest on mortgages and chattels against their income before they calculate income tax. Here we do not have that privilege. The net result is that in the United States a person can now have a $40,000 mortgage with a 25-year amortization period with monthly payments of $331 per month, whereas in Canada the monthly payment is almost $100 higher, $412 a month for the same size mortgage on the same amortization over a 25-year period. An average Canadian must now pay $123,000 to clear off a $40,000 mortgage, whereas the average American with a $40,000 mortgage would pay $99,000.
I think the government should become a little more honest with the Canadian public concerning the dilemma it is in. By increasing the debt charges in this nation by a half point recently the government has increased the overall cost to Canadians in respect of borrowing money by $350 million approximately. I calculate that figure simply based on the $70 million outstanding debt insofar as our

March 15, 1976
Adjournment Debate
Canadian banks are concerned at the present time. Such an increase in interest rates is inflationary, not deflationary.
The Minister of Finance's contention that he is effectively restraining the growth of our money system by the increase in the interest rate is absolute nonsense. Sure; that perhaps has an indirect slowing down on the demand for money but it does not have the effect of increasing the reserves that are required by the chartered banks with regard to their loan activity. That is the effective way to bring monetary expansion in line.

subtopic: FINANCE-EFFECT OF RAISING BANK INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the
announcement of the increase in the bank rate from 9 to 91/2 per cent, made on March 5 by the Bank of Canada, chartered banks announced similar increases in their prime rate which is now established at 1014 per cent. At the same time, banks increased their rates on savings accounts by at least V4 or 1 per cent. It is still too early to know the full impact of this increase on other interest rates, particularly on mortgages and personal loans.
As far as the personal loans rate is concerned, I would like to underline that this rate does not necessarily always vary according to the same pattern as the banks' prime rate. So when we consider the movement of interest rates from early 1973 to the end of 1974, we see that the consumer loans rate increased by only 1 to IV2 per cent, while during the same period the prime rate went up 514 per cent. There may be several reasons for the difference between these two markets, including-not least- administrative matters concerning banks.
It is enough, within the ambit of this discussion, to recall that the personal loan market may not be affected by rising prime rates in the same way as business loans are.
The rate for consumer loans now authorized by the banks stands around 13 lA per cent.
Mortgage rates, on the other hand, respond more readily to the variations of the basic bank rate and we can expect some increase in this field. This is because mortgage rates are generally determined by the rates which lenders must pay on term deposits which are their main source of funding. Now banks have not yet announced changes in the interest rates on term deposits. On the other hand, a few trust companies have already announced rate increases in their guaranteed investment certificates. Those increases vary from 14 of 1 per cent to % of 1 per cent. Those companies have raised their mortgage rates by 14 of one per cent, which means they now reach the 12 per cent ceiling they had reached recently. Therefore it is too early to predict at what exact level those mortgage rates will level off.
I would like to point out two interesting facts concerning this recent increase in the bank interest rates. First, we must rejoice at the fact that some banks have reestablished a special rate for small concerns. This lower prime rate for small concerns allows them to better face the effects of higher interest rates. It is to be hoped that all the banks will reestablish this special rate.
Second, I would like to draw the attention of the House on the fact that some banks have already announced increases in interest rates paid on savings which exceed the increases in interest rates charged on loans, thus reducing profit margins. I hope that the anti-inflation program of the government has contributed to this reduction of bank profits to the benefit of those who make savings.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, although we may have to wait a little longer before we have a true and complete picture of the repercussions of the recent increase in interest rates, we can already notice some encouraging signs concerning the reestablishment of a special treatment for small concerns and a decrease in bank profits.
